title: Sarcoidosis: A Comprehensive Ophthalmic & Systemic Guide
summary: A relatively common, potentially life-threatening granulomatous multisystem disorder of unknown cause. This poster details the ophthalmic manifestations, systemic involvement, diagnostic investigations, and treatment strategies for Sarcoidosis.

sections.title: At-Risk Populations & Etiology
sections.content: Sarcoidosis is a relatively common granulomatous multisystem disorder that may be life-threatening. It affects up to 0.1% of the population, being higher in ♀ and with peaks in the third and sixth decades. It is commoner in African-Caribbeans, Irish, and Scandinavians. The cause is unknown; there is PCR evidence for several agents (including atypical mycobacteria) that may trigger the disease in susceptible individuals. The Th1 response predominates in typical sarcoidosis granulomata, although it appears that a transition to the Th2 response underlies progressive pulmonary fibrosis.

rows: Erythema nodosum and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL)
Better prognosis; tends to be self-limiting

branches: Anterior Uveitis: 2/3 persistent, 1/3 acute; unilateral or bilateral; 'granulomatous'; circumlimbal injection, mutton fat KPs, AC flare/cells, PS, vitreous cells; iris granulomas and nodules.
Intermediate Uveitis: Vitreous cells, snowballs, snowbanking.

Posterior Uveitis: CMO (commonest cause of dVA), periphlebitis (± patchy sheathing ± 'candle wax dripping'), occluded vessels (especially BRVO), neovascularization, choroidal/retinal/preretinal nodules (probably granulomata), pigment epithelial changes, disc swelling (from inflammatory papillitis, optic nerve granuloma, or papilloedema 2° to CNS disease).
Diagnostic Sign: Peripheral multifocal chorioretinitis (small punched-out atrophic spots) are highly suggestive of sarcoidosis.
Complications: Cataract, glaucoma (↑ risk with duration of active disease), CNV.

sections.title: Systemic Clinical Features
content: Respiratory (RS): Often asymptomatic despite CXR changes, dry cough, dyspnoea; BHL, parenchymal disease.
Cardiovascular (CVS): Pericarditis, cardiomyopathy, conduction defects, cardiac failure, cor pulmonale.

Skin: Erythema nodosum (red, tender, elevated lesions typically on shins; commonest in younger ♀); cutaneous granulomata (non-tender nodules/papules/macules, almost anywhere including lids); lupus pernio (uncommon bluish plaque on face/ears).
Joints: Arthritis (commoner in acute sarcoidosis); bone cysts (usually in digits).
Glands: Swelling of lacrimal, salivary, parotid, and submaxillary glands; lymphadenopathy; hepatosplenomegaly.

CNS (Neurosarcoidosis): Commoner in patients with posterior uveitis; cranial nerve palsies (most commonly VIIn; can be bilateral), peripheral neuropathy, myopathy, aseptic meningoencephalitis (typically basal leptomeninges); CNS granuloma may mimic a tumour; optic nerve involvement may present as an atypical optic neuritis.

sections.title: Primary Investigations
content: Diagnosis: Essentially clinical but supported by ACE, imaging, and histology. Difficult to distinguish neurosarcoidosis from MS in some cases.
Serum ACE: Commonly elevated in active disease due to activated macrophages; synthesis. False negatives in patients on ACE inhibitors.
Serum Ca2+: Less commonly elevated.
CXR: Abnormal in >90% with ocular sarcoid.
HRCT Thorax: High sensitivity and specificity; useful if CXR is normal.
MRI Brain/Optic Nerves: Fat-suppressed, gadolinium-enhanced T1 and LP for suspected neurosarcoid.

sections.title: CXR Staging
content: Stage 0: Normal
Stage 1: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL) only
Stage 2: BHL + parenchymal disease
Stage 3: Parenchymal disease only

sections.title: Advanced Diagnostic Imaging
content: Gallium-67 scan: Typical uptake pattern is lacrimal and parotid glands (panda appearance) or mediastinum (lambda sign).

PET-CT scan: PET captures images of minuscule changes in metabolism caused by growth of abnormal cells; CT allows exact location, size, and shape pinpointing. Small lesions (e.g. lymph nodes) detected with PET and located with CT.
FFA (Fundus Fluorescein Angiography): Includes ischaemia (hypofluorescence), leakage from periphlebitis, new vessels, CMO (hyperfluorescence).
ICG (Indocyanine Green): Choroidal stromal vasculitis, early lobular hypofluorescence, late hyperfluorescence (focal or diffuse).

sections.title: Biopsy and Histology
sections.content: Biopsy (transbronchial, endobronchial, or conjunctival) may reveal the typical non-caseating granulomata of whorls of epithelioid cells surrounding multinucleate giant cells. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) may show lymphocytosis with high CD4+/CD8+ ratio, but has low specificity.

sections.title: Box 11.3: Differential Diagnosis of Elevated Serum ACE
content: Child (peaks at 13y of age, adult level by 18y)
Sarcoidosis
Mycobacterial infection (including leprosy and TB)
Chronic lung diseases (berylliosis, silicosis, farmer’s lung, histoplasmosis, lymphangiomyomatosis)
Gaucher’s disease

sections.title: Treatment of Ophthalmic Disease
content: Anterior Segment: Treated as for idiopathic AAU (Acute Anterior Uveitis).
Posterior Segment: Treated as for intermediate uveitis.
Cataract: Conventional surgery with tight control of inflammation.
Glaucoma: Medical ± surgical (augmented trabeculectomy/tube).
CNV: Intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy or intravitreal corticosteroid.

content.explanation: Heerfordt’s syndrome (uveoparotid fever): Parotid/submandibular gland enlargement, VIIn palsy, uveitis. Löfgren’s syndrome: Fever, erythema nodosum, BHL. Mickulicz’s syndrome: Diffuse swelling of lacrimal/salivary glands (most commonly due to sarcoidosis).
